title: National Single Window for Trade goes live after 30-year wait | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 5

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma (standing, centre) at the launch of OneTRADE, the National Single Window for Trade

Nearly 30 years since the project was first mooted, the National Single Window for Trade, an online portal intended to replace duplicated paper filings to Customs, quarantine, port and other agencies with a single submission, went live this week with two export sectors admitted and no timetable published for the rest.

A private sector exporter created the first Customs Declaration (CusDec) through the platform on the launch day on Thursday (5) the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry said.

Onboarding is sector by sector, beginning with coconut and tea. The Treasury said the system would be opened to other sectors “in the near future” once it “is further refined based on the go-live findings”. No date was given.

The portal, branded OneTRADE, is a joint initiative of the Finance Ministry, the Ministry of Digital Economy and GovTech Sri Lanka Ltd., a state-owned software company. The Lanka Software Foundation supported the build.

A single window is required under Article 10.4 of the World Trade Organisation’s Trade Facilitation Agreement. Sri Lanka submitted its instrument of ratification on 31 May 2016, becoming the 81st member to do so. Its implementation of agreement commitments, measured by the WTO, stands at 34.9% against a schedule running to 2030.

The project has moved slowly since work began in 1993. The World Bank completed a 12-volume blueprint in 2018, but the documents were mislaid and had to be resubmitted in July 2019. Cabinet approved a phased rollout with World Bank funding only in June 2022, and the Government allocated Rs. 200 million in June 2023 to establish a project implementation unit.

Comparable systems abroad give a measure of the potential gain. A World Bank study cited by the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce found single windows cut import and export processing time by 30-40%. Singapore’s TradeNet reduced processing from four days to 10 minutes, and South Korea’s system cut transaction costs by 60%.

For exporters the immediate effect is administrative, replacing counter visits and repeat submissions with one lodgement. Whether the savings materialise depends on how many agencies are connected, which the Ministry has not disclosed.

title: Govt. to reapply for GSP+ under EU’s new 10-year framework | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 5

Finance Deputy Minister 

Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando

Finance Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando told Parliament that the Government will reapply for trade concessions under the European Union’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) to retain preferential access to the bloc’s market beyond 2027.

GSP+ is the EU’s most generous tariff arrangement for developing countries, cutting duties to zero on around two thirds of product lines in return for binding commitments to 27 international conventions covering human rights, labour standards, environmental protection and good governance.

Answering Opposition MP Ravi Karunanayake in Parliament on Thursday, Dr. Fernando said the EU’s renewed GSP framework takes effect on 1 January, 2027 and remains in operation until 31 December, 2036.

Beneficiaries of the current scheme must submit fresh applications under the new framework, though they may continue on existing terms during a transition period running to the end of 2028. Sri Lanka will file within the window from 1 January, 2027 to 31 December, 2028 and is working to meet the conditions needed to keep GSP+ status, Dr. Fernando said. 

The concessions matter most to apparel, the country’s largest export earner, which competes in the EU against suppliers paying standard tariffs. The previous GSP+ arrangement ran to the end of 2023 and was extended pending the revision now in force from January.

The Joint Apparel Associations Forum (JAAF) recently warned that the Government’s proposed anti-terror Bill is ‘very likely to be a roadblock’ to that (GSP+) application.

Apparel earns about $ 5 billion a year and more than 40% of merchandise exports, and the EU absorbs a little over 30% of the total, including $ 705 million in the first half of 2026, a period in which those shipments fell 8% while EU imports of apparel from China rose 5% and from Vietnam 9%.

JAAF does not argue against a counter-terrorism law. However, it points out that a Bill this broad, with so little judicial oversight, puts at risk the trade access that sustains hundreds of thousands of livelihoods, because GSP+ is conditional on compliance with 27 international conventions and the EU will weigh the replacement law when Sri Lanka reapplies for the scheme’s next cycle in 2027. 

The industry body argues that a failed application would leave the country without its largest trade preference program, and that amending the Bill now is cheap where fixing it afterwards will not be.

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma (right) exchanges the agreement signed with ADB Sri Lanka Residence Mission Country Director Shannon Cowlin

The Government yesterday signed a $ 100 million policy-based loan with the Asian Development Bank to fund the second phase of a water sector reform program, with the money routed to the Budget against agreed policy actions rather than to pipelines or plants.

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma signed for the Government and ADB Sri Lanka Residence Mission Country Director Shannon Cowlin for the lender at the General Treasury in Colombo.

The package comprises a $ 50 million concessional loan and $ 50 million from the ADB’s ordinary capital resources, under the Water Supply and Sanitation Reform Program, Subprogram 2.

The Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry said the program backs reforms to water resources governance, drinking water safety, sanitation management, conservation, tariff and financial sustainability, and private sector participation and climate finance mobilisation.

The program is the first policy-based lending operation in the water sector. Subprogram 1, also $ 100 million, closed in 2024 having set the policy, regulatory and institutional foundations. The second phase is meant to implement and deepen them.

The Housing, Construction and Water Supply is the executing agency and also an implementing agency, alongside the Prime Minister’s Office and the National Water Supply and Drainage Board (NWSDB).

title: CPC rules out fuel shortage | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 4

The Ceylon Petroleum Corporation yesterday said there is no fuel shortage, after private distributors cut volumes and queues formed in areas without a nearby State filling station.

The CPC said reserves were adequate and that it was releasing stock continuously through its Ceypetco network, with distribution uninterrupted. The corporation said the problem was not supply but the withdrawal of volumes by certain private companies, which it attributed to their operational losses. Long queues had formed where no Ceypetco station operates nearby, it said.

The CPC said 52 such locations had been identified and that at a meeting chaired by the Secretary with all fuel companies, the firms agreed to prioritise supplies to those areas when distributing available stocks.

It said the companies had confirmed their reduced volumes were down to losses, and had now undertaken to serve the designated locations first. CPC said minor queues may still appear in places where private distribution has fallen, but that it had raised its own volumes to compensate and there was no disruption or deficit in distribution.

title: Shanakiyan questions Rs. 41 b fuel subsidy as CPC books Rs. 29.2 b profit | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 6

MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam

Ilankai Tamil Arasu Katchi (ITAK) MP Shanakiyan Rasamanickam yesterday questioned in Parliament whether the Rs. 41 billion in Treasury fuel subsidies had reached consumers, and pointed to a Rs. 29.2 billion net profit at the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) over the same period.

Addressing the House, Rasamanickam asked whether the full benefit of the April to June 2026 allocation had been passed through in lower pump prices, and whether the state oil monopoly’s purpose was to earn profit or to supply affordable fuel.

The corporation’s profit and the subsidy cover the same quarter.

Rasamanickam challenged Deputy Minister Kaushalya Ariyarathne’s statement that fuel is sold below import cost, citing figures of Rs. 307 a litre for imported diesel and Rs. 322 for petrol, and seeking a comparison with prevailing retail prices and the pricing formula.

Citing the Finance Ministry’s Mid-Year Fiscal Position Report, Rasamanickam said the Treasury held a cash balance of Rs. 690.3 billion at the end of June 2026, and asked why further taxes were being levied on fuel against reserves of that size.

The MP sought the total subsidy allocated since January, the split between the CPC and private distributors, and monthly outlays on fuel and electricity relief. He asked whether the Rs. 70 a litre diesel subsidy would run past 31 December, 2026.

A further Rs. 41 billion has already been approved to subsidise Auto Diesel and Industrial Diesel across October, November and December.

Rasamanickam said headline inflation reached 8.3% in October and food inflation 8.8%, and warned that costlier diesel would drive up production costs in the coming Maha season.

He pressed for targeted relief for farmers, fishermen and public transport operators, arguing it would reach households and productive sectors faster than a blanket subsidy, and that support for bus operators would ease fares.

Rasamanickam demanded disclosure of how the subsidy money has been spent and whether it has reached consumers.

Jinasena Ltd., has launched its Fire and Safety Projects Division, marking a strategic expansion into the fire protection and safety sector. 

The move extends the company’s established engineering expertise into Sri Lanka’s commercial, industrial and institutional infrastructure, with a comprehensive range of fire detection, protection and suppression solutions.  

Jinasena Ltd., Managing Director, Shani Jinasena said:  “Responsible building and infrastructure development has always included fire safety as an important aspect. In order to provide customers with a more comprehensive approach to fire protection, we are combining our engineering expertise and reliable service capabilities with existing fire pump solutions with this new division. Our goal is to offer reliable, end-to-end solutions that meet organisations’ fire safety needs, from system design and installation to testing and ongoing maintenance.”

The Fire and Safety Projects Division offers addressable, conventional and wireless fire alarm systems, aspirating smoke detection, portable fire extinguishers, hydrants and hose reels, listed and non-listed fire pump sets, fire-rated doors, and sprinkler and valve systems. Specialised suppression solutions include water mist, clean agent, carbon dioxide (CO2), foam and kitchen wet-chemical systems.  

Each project follows a three-step approach: risk assessment, solution design, and verification through installation, commissioning and testing before handover. Systems with UL and LPCB approvals are designed and installed in line with recognised international standards, such as NFPA, BS EN, and SLS/ISO. From initial surveys and design to installation, commissioning, and maintenance, lifecycle support is provided.    

Founded in 1905, Jinasena Ltd., is one of Sri Lanka’s oldest and most respected domestic and industrial water pump manufacturers. Customised Pumps, Water Purification, Irrigation, Solar, and IT solutions are all part of its portfolio. The company’s engineering capabilities are further extended into the infrastructure and building fire protection requirements by the Fire and Safety Projects Division.    

Safeguarding building occupants, protecting physical assets, and reducing the possibility of operational disruption are all made possible by effective fire protection. Through solutions designed to meet the needs of commercial and office buildings, manufacturing and industrial facilities, retail and hospitality establishments, healthcare and educational institutions, infrastructure and utilities, and residential developments, the division seeks to support these priorities.

Property developers, building owners, construction firms, main contractors, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) contractors, architects, engineers, consultants, and procurement teams engaged in infrastructure and building projects are among its potential client base. 

Under the leadership of Chief Operating Officer Guyanga Weerasekera, Chief Sales and Marketing Officer Chinthaka Wickramasinghe, and Head of the Fire and Safety Projects Division Anoj Kaluarachchi, Jinasena (Pvt) Ltd seeks to strengthen its position in the fire and safety sector and establish enduring relationships with institutional, corporate, and infrastructure stakeholders.

title: John Keells Properties and John Keells  Stock Brokers bring real estate and capital markets together at ‘The Investment Playbook’ | Daily FT

John Keells Properties, in collaboration with John Keells Stock Brokers, hosted ‘The Investment Playbook’, an exclusive, invitation-only investment forum that brought together perspectives from real estate, equity markets and wealth management to explore how investors can build long-term wealth through a more diversified approach to investing.

Held on 29 October 2026 at The Residences at Cinnamon Life under the theme “The Investment Playbook - Rethinking Wealth Across Markets”, the forum challenged the conventional view of real estate and equities as competing investment choices, exploring instead how both asset classes can complement one another within a well-structured portfolio. Leading voices from the financial services and real estate sectors examined the economic forces shaping investment decisions, emerging opportunities within Sri Lanka’s capital markets, and the enduring role of property in long-term wealth creation.

The evening opened with a regional market outlook from Maybank Investment Banking Group Head of Research and Regional Head of Financials Thilan Wickramasinghe. Drawing on over two decades of experience across international financial institutions, Wickramasinghe offered a broader perspective on regional economic developments, interest rates and capital flows, and their implications for investors in Sri Lanka.

John Keells Stock Brokers Head of Research Navin Ratnayake then turned to the relationship between equities and underlying real estate assets, examining the significance of land and property holdings within publicly listed companies and the importance of understanding underlying asset values when evaluating investment opportunities. His segment highlighted how investors can gain exposure to real estate both through direct property ownership and through the equity market.

This was followed by a panel discussion, led by Navin Ratnayake, featuring John Keells Property Group Chief Commercial Officer and John Keells Holdings Senior Vice President Nadeem Shums, and LYNEAR Wealth CEO of Unit Trusts and Head of Equities Asanka Herath. The panel explored the investment characteristics of equities and real estate, the factors influencing valuations, and the importance of balancing capital appreciation, income generation, liquidity and risk when making long-term investment decisions.

Commenting on the event, Nadeem Shums said: “Real estate has always played a significant role in how Sri Lankans create and preserve wealth. However, the conversation around property investment needs to evolve beyond simply purchasing an apartment or acquiring land. Investors today are increasingly looking at capital appreciation, rental income, location fundamentals and the long-term value of the assets they hold. At John Keells Properties, we believe that well-planned developments in strategic locations can play an important role in long-term wealth creation. Through events such as The Investment Playbook, we want to encourage investors to look at property within the context of their broader investment portfolios and make decisions based on a deeper understanding of value.”

John Keells Stock Brokers Chief Executive Officer and John Keells Holdings Vice President Nithila Talgaswatte added: “Successful investing is not necessarily about choosing one asset class over another. It is about understanding how different investments behave, the risks and opportunities they present, and how they can work together to achieve an individual’s financial objectives. Equities allow investors to participate in the growth of businesses, protect yourself with dividend yield and can also give exposure to underlying real estate owned by a listed company, while real estate offers tangible asset ownership, income potential and long-term value. By bringing these perspectives together, we hope to encourage a more holistic approach to investing, driven by research, diversification and long-term financial planning.”

The collaboration reflects a shared effort to encourage informed investment decisions by bringing together expertise from different segments of the investment landscape. For John Keells Properties, the initiative forms part of a broader commitment to engaging with investors beyond individual property transactions, creating space for meaningful conversations around investment strategy, market developments and long-term value. For John Keells Stock Brokers, it reinforces the importance of investment education, market research and informed decision-making in an increasingly dynamic financial landscape.

As economic conditions and financial markets continue to evolve, The Investment Playbook reinforced a central message: long-term wealth is not built by choosing between asset classes, but by understanding how each contributes to a broader investment strategy.

The evening concluded with an informal networking session, giving attendees the opportunity to engage with the speakers and continue the investment conversation.

title: International partnership to strengthen hydrogen higher education in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 13

Building on a decade-long partnership in Higher Education and  Research on Clean Energy Technologies (HRNCET) between the University of Jaffna, Sri  Lanka, and Western Norway University of Applied Sciences (HVL), Norway, a new  international initiative will further strengthen Sri Lanka’s capacity in hydrogen education  and research. 

The Green Hydrogen Enabling Technologies (GREEN-HET) project will be formally  launched on 10 November 2026 at Jetwing Colombo Seven Hotel, under the patronage of Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya, who will grace the  occasion as the Chief Guest. The event will bring together international academic  partners and key stakeholders from government, industry, the diplomatic community and  wider society. 

Funded by the European Union (EU) through its Erasmus+ Capacity Building in Higher  Education (CBHE) program, GREEN-HET is a three-year initiative aimed at  developing a joint Master’s degree program in Hydrogen Enabling Technologies across  four Sri Lankan universities, while strengthening national expertise, higher education  capacity and institutional collaboration in the emerging hydrogen sector. 

The Master’s program will be jointly developed and delivered under the national  coordination of the University of Jaffna, with the participation of the Universities of  Moratuwa, Peradeniya and Ruhuna. The European consortium comprises HVL, Norway;  the University of Groningen, the Netherlands; OTH Regensburg – Technical University of  Applied Sciences, Germany; and Virumaa College of Tallinn University of Technology,  Estonia. 

Western Norway University of Applied Sciences (HVL) is the applicant institution and  overall project coordinator of GREEN-HET. HVL led the preparation and submission of the  successful project proposal and now coordinates the eight-university consortium. The  project builds on HVL’s internationally recognised expertise in hydrogen technologies  and its longstanding academic and research collaboration with Sri Lankan universities,  established and strengthened through Norwegian-supported initiatives. 

Through this international partnership, the consortium will jointly develop the  curriculum, enhance academic staff competencies, strengthen laboratory facilities and  establish shared teaching resources and quality assurance mechanisms. Academic  training programs and industrial visits in Europe will provide Sri Lankan academics  with opportunities to exchange knowledge and experience with leading university and  industry specialists and adapt international best practices to the country’s specific  needs. 

The proposed curriculum will address the entire hydrogen value chain, covering hydrogen  production, storage, transportation, fuel cells and integration with renewable energy  systems. It will also incorporate essential interdisciplinary areas, including hydrogen  safety, environmental assessment, techno-economic analysis, policy and regulation,  modelling and digital technologies. The European partner institutions will contribute  complementary expertise in hydrogen technologies, advanced materials and  sustainable energy systems. 

The project is particularly relevant to Sri Lanka’s national energy transition ambitions and  the priorities outlined in its National Hydrogen Roadmap. With considerable renewable  energy potential, Sri Lanka has opportunities to explore green hydrogen and green  ammonia production, enhance energy security and develop potential domestic and  international markets. By developing a skilled workforce and strengthening institutional  expertise, GREEN-HET will help the country assess and harness these opportunities  based on sound technical, economic and environmental considerations. 

An important component of the project will be the establishment of a National Hydrogen  Forum, bringing together universities, industry representatives, government authorities  and civil society organisations. Through stakeholder consultations, seminars,  knowledge-sharing activities and public outreach programs, the Forum will facilitate  dialogue, promote awareness, inform curriculum development and foster sustainable  collaboration among national stakeholders beyond the project’s funding period. 

For young people in Sri Lanka, the initiative will create valuable opportunities to access  internationally informed postgraduate education within the country, acquire practical  knowledge and engage in research addressing emerging needs in the energy sector. The  joint delivery of the program across four Sri Lankan universities will enable students  to benefit from the combined academic expertise, research capabilities and laboratory  facilities of the participating institutions. 

The inaugural ceremony is expected to bring together invited ministers, senior  government officials, diplomatic representatives, representatives of the European Union,  university leaders, academics, industry professionals and other key stakeholders. A  series of consortium meetings and partner discussions will also be held in connection  with the launch to establish implementation priorities, strengthen institutional  commitments and agree on the next steps towards developing and delivering the joint  Master’s program. 

Through GREEN-HET, Sri Lanka will take an important step towards building the human  capital, academic expertise and international partnerships required to participate in the  emerging global hydrogen economy.

The inaugural session of the two-day Dialogue was attended by Pathfinder Foundation Founder Milinda Moragoda. The session featured a plenary address by Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) Secretary-General Ambassador Indra Mani Pandey, and a keynote address delivered via a recorded message by Indonesia Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Arief Havas Oegroseno. 

A special address was delivered by German Ambassador Dr. Felix Neumann, who highlighted the strategic significance of the Indian Ocean, describing it as a maritime region that connects the global economy and serves as the heartbeat of international commerce.

The Bay of Bengal region, one of the world’s most densely populated and economically dynamic areas, continues to play a pivotal role in global trade and regional development. Approximately a quarter of global maritime commerce passes through its waters, while its considerable natural and human resources offer significant opportunities for sustainable economic growth.

Building on the policy recommendations developed through the five previous Dialogues, this year’s gathering placed particular emphasis on translating policy recommendations into practical and actionable outcomes.

The key thematic priorities included advancing regional consensus on collaborative maritime governance, establishing coordinated mechanisms to strengthen maritime communications, and addressing illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. The Dialogue also sought to deepen understanding of the Bay of Bengal as a distinct sub-region within the broader Indo-Pacific, where geopolitical, economic and ecological interests increasingly converge.

The Sixth Dialogue further incorporated cross-cutting priorities, particularly inclusive policymaking, recognising the importance of grounding maritime security policies in local realities and strengthening scientific collaboration.

Welcome remarks were delivered by Ambassador (Retd.) Bernard Goonetilleke, Chairman of the Pathfinder Foundation, and Ambassador (Retd.) Venu Rajamony, Senior Adviser for South Asia at the Centre for Humanitarian Dialogue.

The two-day event brought together local and international participants, including representatives of diplomatic missions based in Colombo, among them ambassadors and high commissioners, as well as experts and stakeholders engaged in maritime affairs and regional cooperation.

title: RCSS study says Middle East war exposed South Asia’s deep dependence | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 11

A Policy Study, authored by RCSS Researcher Thedini Herath, has found that the 2026 Middle East war did not create, but dramatically exposed how heavily South Asian states depend on a single region. 

It noted that the war hit all five pillars of dependence at once: soaring oil prices raised fuel import bills and strained foreign reserves; the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted the region’s key trade routes; the loss of jobs in the Gulf threatened the livelihoods of tens of millions of South Asian workers; Gulf financing tightened as sovereign wealth funds turned inward; and long-standing politico-strategic partnerships with countries on different sides of the conflict were tested. 

The study called for reducing this over-concentration in order to build long-term resilience in the relationship.

The study titled South Asia’s ‘Middle East Dependency Trap’: How the 2026 Iran War Exposed the Region’s Politico-Economic Vulnerabilities, was presented by the author at the RCSS-MIR joint webinar titled ‘Evolving South Asia–Middle East Relations: Opportunities for Cooperation in a Changing Geopolitical Landscape’, held on 29 October 2026, with a live audience at RCSS, Colombo, and participants joining virtually from the UAE and representatives from Sri Lanka’s diplomatic missions in the Middle East region and scholars across the region. 

The co-chairs of the session welcomed the new partnership between the two institutions, established through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in July 2026. MIR Director of Research Dr. Ahmed Abdel Alim celebrated the rapid movement from discussion to concrete action, observing that the war had created both challenges and opportunities for the two regions and shown how deeply interconnected they are. RCSS Executive Director Ambassador Ravinatha Ariyasinha, while noting that the collaboration extended the RCSS’s reach to the Middle East region, said the policy study also marked the RCSS’s return to theoretical work, offering a timely, in-depth look at South Asia as a whole in relation to the Middle East.

Viewing current developments through the prism of Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye’s concept of ‘complex interdependence’, Herath noted that the study shows that the imbalance in the relationship is a source of vulnerability. However, while Keohane and Nye focus mainly on economic and transnational ties, the study adds ‘politico-strategic partnerships’ as a distinct pillar of interdependence. In a further theoretical contribution, the study emphasises how the present war also points to an additional dimension of vulnerability that may need to be integrated into the interdependence framework. 

While Keohane and Nye’s analysis saw military force as playing only a minor role, and as something the governments in an interdependent relationship might use, whether against each other or against outside powers, rather than treating strategic ties as a channel of interdependence in its own right, South Asia’s interdependence with the Middle East was disrupted by an extraneous force - in a war between the United States, Israel and Iran - in which none of the South Asian countries had any part.

During the open discussion that followed, the extent of the UAE’s contribution to South Asian economies and their resilience during the crisis was discussed, along with how expanded cooperation between the two institutions could play a vital role in these times. Responding, Herath noted that the study recognises these mutual benefits and appreciated the support provided. Turning to the protection of migrant workers, Herath pointed to the potential of existing forums, such as the Colombo Process, which brings together the region’s labour-sending states, and the Abu Dhabi Dialogue, which connects both the sending and receiving countries. She said these platforms could advance skills recognition, ethical recruitment and standard employment contracts, helping move workers out of the most precarious jobs and up the skills ladder. 

It was also noted that while cooperation through multilateral fora between the two regions as a whole remains important, both South Asian and Middle Eastern countries must also work hard to safeguard their respective bilateral relationships, rather than letting them be absorbed into the larger regional relationship, so that the close bilateral relations built over decades are not lost. Asked whether South Asia’s dependence amounted to neo-colonialism, Herath noted that while colonial history helped create the early links, the current dependence was not imposed by a coloniser but was largely built through South Asia’s own choices, which is why the study describes the relationship as asymmetric interdependence. On the options open to small states, she described non-alignment as part of a wider hedging strategy, pointing to Sri Lanka’s own response during the current war: when the Iranian vessel IRIS Dena was sunk off its southern coast, Sri Lanka rescued and assisted the survivors, while also declining both a US request to land warplanes at Mattala and Iranian requests for naval goodwill visits.

title: FSP challenges AKD’s proposed amendments to Organised Crime Act | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00

The Frontline Socialist Party (FSP) has challenged President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s commitment to amend the proposed Organised Crime Act, arguing that the changes he outlined are merely superficial and fail to address the fundamental threats the legislation poses to democratic rights and civil liberties.

Addressing a media briefing yesterday, FSP Education Secretary Pubudu Jayagoda said the President’s remarks at a meeting with religious leaders at Temple Trees on Thursday (5) had focused on three specific provisions, while ignoring the broader concerns raised by trade unions, human rights organisations, professionals and civil society groups.

The President had reportedly described the legislation as non-repressive and formulated in accordance with international standards, while alleging that those opposing it were acting in the interests of underworld groups and criminals.

Jayagoda said the Government had been compelled to reconsider its position following widespread public opposition, including the 4 November protest near Parliament.

“An administration that previously defended the Bill with such rhetoric has reached this level of flexibility only because an entire society raised its voice against this repressive Act,” he said.

He identified three areas addressed by the President and explained why the proposed amendments would not resolve the fundamental problems.

Citing FSP’s first concern as ‘reducing detention from 72 to 48 hours’, Jayagoda said the President’s proposal to reduce the period of police detention from 72 to 48 hours failed to address the extensive powers granted to law enforcement authorities.

He pointed out that the legislation provides for arrests on suspicion of association with criminal gangs, detention orders extending up to one year without judicial review and detention facilities without adequate judicial oversight.

“The problem is not merely the number of hours, but the sweeping, unlimited powers granted to the police by the Act,” he said.

He also criticised provisions that, in his view, reduce magistrates to rubber stamps and transfer judicial authority to the executive.

“Do not bargain over the number of hours like a street vendor. These laws concern the democratic rights of the people,” Jayagoda said.

Responding to the President Dissanayake’s indication that the provision identifying criminal gang members through tattoos would be changed, Jayagoda said the issue went far beyond tattoos.

He argued that the legislation could make individuals suspects based on their physical appearance and social associations rather than evidence of their involvement in criminal activity.

“The tattoo provision is merely a symbol of the ridiculous nature of this Act,” he said, adding that the legislation undermined the fundamental legal principle that criminal liability should be based on an individual’s involvement in an offence.

Jayagoda also questioned the President’s proposal to remove offences under the Excise Ordinance, asking why offences under other laws, including the Betting and Gaming Ordinance, Forest and Flora Ordinance, Wildlife Ordinance and Archaeology Act, were not also being reconsidered.

He warned that even people participating in protests could potentially be classified as organised criminals through provisions relating to obstructing public officers in the performance of their duties.

Jagoda further questioned why the President had not addressed provisions concerning police-obtained confessions, access to private communications and electronic devices, and the criminalisation of past associations with suspected organised criminals.

He also criticised the Government for remaining silent on the proposed State Terrorism Act (PSTA), arguing that it could not be adequately corrected through amendments and should be withdrawn, alongside the repeal of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA).

Jagoda urged the President to engage with trade unions, student organisations, human rights activists, lawyers and communities affected by the proposed legislation rather than limiting discussions to Buddhist monks, Catholic priests and Hindu and Muslim clergies. 

“Separate religion from the state. These matters should not be discussed with crowds forcibly assembled at Temple Trees by mobilising  the authority of Divisional Secretaries. Instead, meet and talk with the labour movement, the student movement, human rights activists, and professionals—including lawyers who have fought for democratic rights for generations,” he stressed.

Jagoda suggested the Government to hold discussions on this issue with the youth of urban poor families in areas like Central Colombo, Wanathamulla, Maligawatta, Modara, Mattakkuliya, and Dematagoda who voted for the NPP and also with female workers of Free Trade Zones.

“Instead of turning your back on your own history and the forces that sustained you, be humble enough to admit when a mistake has been made and correct it,” he said.

The Election Commission has told the warring factions of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party that the party can no longer be treated as a formally recognised political party, 75 years after S.W.R.D. Bandaranaike founded it as an alternative to the United National Party.

The Commission has directed both sides to submit a fresh application for registration and to satisfy the criteria, foremost among them the holding of a proper party election.

Recognition is the gate to contesting under a party’s name and symbol, to nominating candidates and to the state entitlements that follow, including broadcast time and National List seats. The SLFP now holds none of these until it re-registers.

The party dominated Sri Lankan politics for half a century. Bandaranaike, its founder, was Prime Minister from 1956 until his assassination in 1959. His widow Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world’s first woman Prime Minister in 1960 and held the office three times. Their daughter Chandrika Bandaranaike Kumaratunga served as President from 1994 to 2005, Mahinda Rajapaksa from 2005 to 2015 and Maithripala Sirisena from 2015 to 2019.
