title: Is AKD running faster than the winds that buffet him? | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:10
-     - 5

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

President Dissanayake still has an opportunity to demonstrate that the NPP’s original commitments were more than an electoral promise. The NPP came to power promising to dismantle a system characterised by concentrated political power, weakened accountability and institutional privilege. It must now decide whether it intends to transform that system or merely occupy it. The greatest danger for the NPP is not necessarily losing power at the next election. It is losing the democratic purpose and moral credibility that brought it to power in the first place

The late Dr. Colvin R. de Silva, the distinguished constitutional lawyer, Marxist politician and political thinker, once made a memorable observation about his contemporary and former classmate, J.R. Jayewardene, architect of Sri Lanka’s Executive Presidency and the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA): “The problem with Dickie is that often he runs faster than the winds that buffet him.” Veteran journalist Sarath De Alwis recently recalled this observation in the Daily FT.

Watching President Anura Kumara Dissanayake (AKD) navigate the complexities of governance, one is tempted to ask the same question: Is AKD running faster than the winds that buffet him?

There is an uncomfortable irony in Sri Lankan politics. The National People’s Power (NPP), elected in 2024 on an extraordinary mandate for democratic renewal, institutional accountability and the abolition of oppressive legislation, is now proposing two controversial Bills: the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA) and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCA). Both have generated serious concerns among constitutional lawyers, human rights organisations and civil society.

Their stated objectives—protecting national security and combating organised crime—are legitimate. No responsible Government can ignore terrorism, drug trafficking or threats to public safety. The fundamental question, however, is whether the proposed means risk undermining the democratic freedoms the Government promised to restore.

From abolishing oppressive laws to creating new instruments of coercion

The NPP’s electoral appeal rested substantially on breaking with the political practices of the past. Its manifesto promised to abolish oppressive legislation, protect fundamental rights and establish accountable democratic governance.

The PTA, introduced in 1979 as a temporary measure, became one of the most controversial instruments of State power in Sri Lanka’s modern history. Successive administrations used it in circumstances involving arbitrary arrests, prolonged detention and the suppression of dissent. The JVP itself experienced the consequences of State repression and emergency legislation.

Yet the proposed replacement legislation raises an uncomfortable question: has the Government genuinely reconsidered the architecture of coercive State power, or is it simply seeking to administer that architecture under different statutory names?

The Centre for Policy Alternatives and the Bar Association of Sri Lanka have raised serious concerns about the Bills, particularly their broad provisions, detention powers and potential restrictions on fundamental freedoms. On 30 October 2026, the UN Human Rights Office called for substantive redrafting of the PSTA, warning of provisions that could reproduce or expand weaknesses associated with the previous legislation.

The constitutional challenges to POCA have also brought these concerns into sharp focus. During the Supreme Court proceedings, President’s Counsel Saliya Pieris and other senior lawyers questioned provisions concerning identification of alleged criminal-group membership, detention, bail and judicial supervision. The inclusion of characteristics such as clothing, tattoos, associations and personal appearance raises an important question: how much discretion should Police officers possess when deciding whom to arrest?

A democratic Government cannot rely merely on assurances that extraordinary powers will not be abused. It must establish safeguards that prevent their misuse by this administration or any Government that follows.

The Executive Presidency:

An inheritance that refuses to disappear

The contradiction extends beyond security legislation. The JVP and NPP spent years condemning the concentration of executive authority under the presidential system and promising its abolition. Yet, the present administration continues to exercise the considerable powers of that very institution, reinforced by its parliamentary supermajority.

Constitutional reform requires careful preparation and public consultation. Delay alone does not establish abandonment of a commitment. Nevertheless, there is a fundamental difference between taking time to design a better constitutional order and allowing inherited executive authority to become politically convenient.

The real test of democratic renewal is not how effectively a Government exercises power when it commands a parliamentary majority, but whether it is prepared to establish institutions capable of restraining its own authority.

Political movements can gradually become protective of the very institutional privileges they once challenged. The danger is that the practical demands of governing may turn temporary concentrations of power into permanent political conveniences.

Economic recovery is not economic prosperity

There is, however, an equally important question that deserves greater attention: what is happening to the economic transformation that brought the NPP to power?

Sri Lanka’s economic catastrophe in 2022, declining living standards and widespread frustration with corruption created the conditions for an unprecedented political transformation. Citizens wanted not merely different political leadership, but a fundamentally different economic future.

To be fair, the Government has maintained important elements of macroeconomic stabilisation. According to the World Bank’s October 2026 Sri Lanka Development Update, the economy expanded by 4.7% in the first half of 2026, with projected growth of 4.4% in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027. Real GDP has returned to pre-crisis levels.

These achievements deserve recognition. Nevertheless, the same assessment estimates poverty at 16.9% in 2025, substantially above pre-crisis levels. Household welfare, real incomes and employment opportunities continue to lag behind the broader recovery.

This is the distinction the Government must confront: macroeconomic stabilisation is not synonymous with economic prosperity.

A fiscal surplus does not automatically translate into better hospitals, functioning schools or completed infrastructure. Higher tax revenue does not necessarily create employment. Debt restructuring does not, by itself, restore household purchasing power.

The 2027 Budget, scheduled for presentation on 12 November, is therefore a critical test. Sri Lanka needs more than revenue mobilisation and fiscal consolidation. It needs productive public investment, stronger exports, private-sector confidence, technological advancement, employment generation and meaningful relief for households struggling with living costs.

Economic discipline must be a foundation for development, not an end in itself.

When economic necessity becomes political convenience

This brings us to a wider political-economic concern. Can a Government sustain an economic programme that imposes considerable adjustments on the population without ensuring that citizens experience tangible improvements?

Emeritus Professor of Economics at the University of Peradeniya, Sumanasiri Liyanage, recently explored this question in the Daily FT,

drawing upon Italian political economist Clara E. Mattei’s influential book, The Capital Order: How Economists Invented Austerity and Paved the Way to Fascism.

Mattei’s historical analysis examines how austerity policies and coercive political institutions can reinforce one another when economic restructuring generates resistance. Her argument is not that every program of fiscal consolidation is authoritarian, but that economic policies imposing unequal social costs can, under certain political circumstances, be supported by increasingly restrictive instruments of State power.

Sri Lanka’s circumstances are not identical to those of Fascist Italy, and simplistic historical comparisons would be intellectually careless. Nevertheless, the underlying institutional question deserves attention.

Workers must retain their right to organise, trade unions must be free to negotiate, journalists must be able to investigate, and citizens must be able to protest peacefully. The State must distinguish genuine terrorism and organised criminality from democratic opposition, industrial action and legitimate public criticism.

If security legislation creates an environment in which resistance to economic policies becomes increasingly difficult, the consequences would extend far beyond individual civil liberties. They would undermine the democratic foundations upon which economic and social reform must rest.

Business confidence requires institutional confidence

The implications are equally important for the business community. Investment depends not merely on attractive tax rates or financial incentives, but on predictable regulations, independent Courts,

transparent administration and confidence in the protection of commercial and individual rights.

Sri Lanka cannot realistically expect to attract foreign investment, expand exports and encourage entrepreneurship, 

while creating uncertainty about the boundaries of executive and police authority.

The Government’s economic programme requires private-sector participation. Democratic accountability and economic confidence are therefore complementary objectives, not competing priorities.

The choice before AKD

President Dissanayake still has an opportunity to demonstrate that the NPP’s original commitments were more than an electoral promise.

Both proposed Bills should undergo genuine public scrutiny, and substantive revision in response to concerns raised by constitutional lawyers, the BASL, human rights organisations and the Supreme Court process. The Government should also establish a credible timetable for constitutional reform, including its commitment to abolish the executive presidency.

Equally important, Budget 2027 must demonstrate how economic recovery will translate into higher real incomes, productive investment,  employment and improved public services. Public expenditure must be judged by delivery, not merely allocations, while accountability must apply equally to present officeholders and their predecessors.

Dr. Colvin R. de Silva’s observation about J.R. Jayewardene remains relevant because political leadership is ultimately tested by its ability to recognise the forces surrounding it.

The NPP came to power promising to dismantle a system characterised by concentrated political power, weakened accountability and institutional privilege. It must now decide whether it intends to transform that system or merely occupy it.

The greatest danger for the NPP is not necessarily losing power at the next election. It is losing the democratic purpose and moral credibility that brought it to power in the first place.

Sri Lanka does not need another Government that believes national security requires excessive State authority or that economic recovery justifies indefinite public sacrifice. It needs leadership confident enough to tolerate criticism, capable enough to transform the economy and principled enough to limit its own powers.

The ultimate measure of AKD’s leadership will not be how effectively he preserves the authority of the State, but how successfully he builds a country in which the State itself is answerable to its citizens.

That is the real promise of political renewal—and the test the NPP must not fail.

title: The new age of ecologically empathetic design | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 11

Since the dawn of civilisation, humans have been talking about developing a better future. Yet, in the memory of every human living today, the quality of life on this planet has been plummeting quite rapidly. The foreground for today’s global decline is an environmental crisis, birthed by our skewed definition of development. If anything is tagged ‘Development’ we blindly destroy the environment; confidently disrupt rivers, carve hillsides and obliterate entire ecosystems. Despite two centuries of practicing development designs intended to beat the environment into submission, we are yet to arrive at this ephemeral ‘better future’. 

Perhaps, if we borrow a design page from the past… and marry it to our sophisticated technology, we will find a hybrid solution for a ‘better future’. A new design ethos that humbly, acknowledges the tremendous power of Nature, is long overdue. Recognition of an ecologically empathetic approach to designing every type of built environment, and the policies that enforce them, is needed. Where better to seed this revised approach to built environments than, through the Trust of the doyen of Sri Lankan architecture, the late Geoffrey Bawa. The Geoffrey Bawa Moonamal Award hopes to inspire this alternate approach to design, from policy to buildings and infrastructure. 

For Sri Lankans, design inspiration is easily sourced, as every remaining precolonial complex is an example of ecologically empathetic design. The only obstacle is our own mental conditioning; unfortunately, even after three quarters of a century of colonial absence, for the majority of Sri Lankans, Western design is their default style. Few have looked back at the colossal design heritage of our island; Minette de Silva, in her early expression of tropical modernism, unravelled the magic of traditional building systems, employing elaborate ventilation, natural lighting and timber joinery. Bawa retrieved the courtyard and sighting precision, as a crucial tropical design feature and further developed his detail, by up-cycling discarded traditional building elements. Many designers have since been inspired, but few have gone beyond the build and applied the sophisticated land-use principals, which once governed our built environments.   

Ancient Sri Lanka’s elegant pavilions, rainwater-harvesting ponds and multiple courtyards were purposefully woven into the canvas of natural environments. Our ancients comprehended nature, beyond the superficial; forests were catchments, ground water was a feeder for cascading reservoirs, rock outcrops were soil stabilisers and prefab hard builds. Ponds were the monsoon’s sponges, urban heat islands were defeated by open paving, courtyards and wooded parklands, water flowed unimpeded beneath raised pavilions…. This is the language of design that we have lost. We also forgot that natural elements are most beneficial, if they are allowed to remain intact or even enhanced. 

In the centuries since we forgot how relevant the natural environment is, focusing on mere buildings instead, we have destroyed landscapes that are key to our survival. Today, the sum total of smaller ecological systems collapsed, by a failed definition of Development, has resulted in Climate Change. Now, planting a few trees or growing monocultures is futile. To move forward, we must restore entire ecosystems — this is rewilding. It is the only solution, if we hope to reap the multiple ecosystem services that natural habitats provide, such as, water storage, air purification, erosion management, soil replenishment, pollination…. Beyond restoration, we need to regenerate new ecosystems, for the lands forever lost to roads, cities, industry and extraction. Regeneration of ecosystems is simply, copy-pasting the primary species of geographically identical, pristine environments, in distressed lands. Unhindered, environments then rapidly restore and regenerate themselves.

The Geoffrey Bawa Moonamal Award, also represents a significant shift from its previous stream, of celebrating independent architects. This big and vital step, will recognise the contribution of multiple skills and knowledge to achieve ecological empathy. The Turkish Nobel laureate, Orhan Parmuk, in My Name is Red, writes of a philosophical conflict between painters of the Ottoman court where fundamentalists condemn the West’s emphasis on individual style. This is the discrepancy, which widened between Eastern and Western perspectives. Eventually, as Western civilisations over-ran older cultures, the celebration of individuals, the soloists who created monumental architecture, rather than deep design through a pooling of knowledge and skills, became the norm. 

Today, as we teeter on the brink of complete ecological collapse, it is finally accepted that enabling ecological harmony requires combining multiple disciplines. Nobody knew this better than Bawa himself, with his coterie of Ena de Silva, Laki Senanayake, Barbara Sansoni, Kandasamy Pulogasunderam et al, who worked in cohesion, to produce a single masterpiece. This is a return to the traditional practice of ateliers of thinkers, designers, technicians and specialised craftspeople. To positively impact our planet, this collaborative approach must encompass infrastructure and policy design too. To “design beyond ourselves” will be a test of ego and a relinquishing of the immense power of the individual designer. 

Who will succeed, will be the designers and developers who interpose rather than impose on landscapes. Advocates of the environment and team players, who read the land and accept that no single individual has the comprehensive knowledge and skills to successfully design and achieve ecological harmony. What is required by architects and developers today, is an understanding that we are now in the age of ecologically empathetic design. This will be the future of global design.

 

(The author’s  design projects include; Jetwing Vil Uyana, Jetwing Kaduruketha, Teardrop’s Camellia Hills etc. She was the first Chair of the Federation of Environmental Organisations, is a member of the Steering Committee of the Geoffrey Bawa Moonamal Award and the author of The Line of Lanka and Ravana’s Lanka. Now retired, she lives in her rewilded monsoon forest, in Central Sri Lanka)

title: The Monk, UNP and Eightfold Path | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 9

The Buddha's first sermon

My article, Beyond the Robe: Sangha, Rule of Law and Monastic Accountability, (https://www.ft.lk/columns/Beyond-the-robe-Sangha-rule-of-law-and-monastic-accountability/4-799100), published on  Saturday, 24 October examined the relationship between Buddhist monastic discipline, institutional responsibility and the rule of law. Subsequently the Daily FT reported that the United National Party (UNP) has "demanded" an immediate Presidential pardon for Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera  (https://www.ft.lk/news/UNP-demands-immediate-presidential-pardon-for-Gnanasara-Thera/56-799219). This would be the second Presidential pardon, that the UNP will be associated with. However, it is about a previous pardon that has been invalidated by the Supreme Court. This presents a further opportunity to elaborate upon what I referred to in the previous article. That is: How might the ethical principles of Buddhism guide political advocacy and the exercise of public power?

Respect for judiciary, principle and BASL

The issue is not whether compassion should be extended to an individual who has been imprisoned. It is whether compassion, accountability, constitutional governance and respect for the judiciary can be pursued together, without allowing political allegiance or religious identity to displace principle. I have not seen any audio or video podcast, Youtube interview, a speech, or statement, from the Bar Association (BASL), to guide political parties, in much the same manner they did with regard to the 22nd Amendment, even writing to urge Parliamentarians to vote with their conscience. 

As for my thoughts of Saturday, 24 October, while I did not think they required further elaboration, perhaps they do. Thus this writing. But first let me reproduce several key points I articulated in my previous article. These were that: 

The issue is bigger than one monk: The controversy is not merely about one individual, one prison decision or one robe; it concerns the relationship between the State, the Sangha, the Constitution and the administration of justice.

The robe deserves respect, but it does not confer immunity: The robe represents renunciation, discipline and commitment. Its significance calls for sensitivity, not exemption from the law.

Criminal liability and monastic status are different matters: A criminal court determines guilt and imposes punishment; the appropriate ecclesiastical authority determines questions of monastic discipline and status.

The State must act lawfully, even with religious institutions: Neither religious identity nor the authority of the State should be used to bypass the Constitution, applicable laws or fair procedures.

The autonomy of the Sangha must be respected: Questions of monastic discipline and status belong within the appropriate ecclesiastical processes, not automatically to political authorities or prison administrators.

Autonomy must go hand in hand with accountability: Religious institutions, like professional bodies and other institutions exercising authority, need credible procedures to investigate allegations, consider evidence and reach fair decisions.

Allegations must be investigated, not presumed: A monk should not be prejudged, but neither should serious allegations of misconduct through words or deeds be dismissed merely because the person wears the robe.

Advocacy must not become intimidation or interference: Religious leaders and public officials may make representations and express reasoned views, but public pressure should never become a substitute for lawful processes or judicial proceedings.

Institutional independence requires safeguards: Intimidation, improper influence and conflicts of interest are legitimate governance risks to examine. Their existence, however, must be established by evidence, not assumed.

Respect and accountability strengthen each other: The dignity of the Sangha is best protected through integrity, compassion, restraint and credible self-discipline—not by placing individuals or institutions beyond scrutiny.

The Noble Eightfold Path - a guide to public conduct

The Noble Eightfold Path is the Buddha's framework for the development of wisdom, ethical conduct and mental discipline. Although traditionally directed towards the cessation of suffering and spiritual development, its ethical principles also offer a valuable framework for reflection on public conduct. Applied thoughtfully to public life, it invites us to examine not only what we seek to achieve, but also our intentions, words and actions.

Right Understanding -

Traditionally, this means understanding the Four Noble Truths. In public life, it also calls for an informed and considered appreciation of the facts, the law and the likely consequences of a demand or decision.

Right Intention – Traditionally, this encompasses renunciation, freedom from ill will and harmlessness. Applied to public conduct, it requires principled motives guided by compassion, fairness and goodwill rather than vengeance, self-interest, political bias or the pursuit of partisan advantage.

Right Speech – This requires abstaining from false, divisive and harsh speech, as well as irresponsible or idle talk. In public life, it calls for truthfulness, restraint and care over the consequences of our words.

Right Action – Traditionally, this requires abstaining from taking life, taking what is not given and sexual misconduct. More broadly, it reminds us that our conduct must be ethically responsible and respectful of the rights of others.

Right Livelihood – This calls for earning one's living through honest and ethical means. Applied to public life, it reminds us that professional and public responsibilities should be exercised with integrity.

Right Effort – This involves preventing unwholesome qualities from arising, abandoning those that have arisen, cultivating wholesome qualities and sustaining their development. In public life, it encourages the consistent practice of ethical conduct and the correction of harmful behaviour.

Right Mindfulness –

Traditionally, this involves mindful awareness of the body, feelings, mind and mental phenomena. In public conduct, it also encourages awareness of our emotions, prejudices and impulses before they influence our decisions and actions.

Right Concentration – This concerns the cultivation of a disciplined and focused mind through meditation. Its wider application to public life may be seen in the value of disciplined, considered judgement and the ability to withstand pressure, and distractions, leading to impulsive reactions, provocation and political expediency.

These are contemporary explanations intended to make the principles accessible to public discussion, not substitutes for their traditional Buddhist meanings. Their application to politics is nevertheless instructive: ethical consistency must be judged not merely by the cause one supports, but also by the motives, words and methods through which that cause is pursued.

Monastic discipline: Conduct through word and deed

As I mentioned in my previous writing, the robe carries moral significance because of the religious vocation and discipline it represents. That significance is sustained by conduct, not by appearance alone. The relevant Nikaya and its governing authorities have an important responsibility to address allegations of monastic misconduct, whether arising from words or deeds, through appropriate, impartial and credible procedures consistent with applicable Vinaya principles and institutional rules.

Responsible advocacy and right intentions

I referred also to the importance of responsible advocacy in my article of Saturday, 24 October. Let me now expand on this. In a democracy, political parties are entitled to advocate clemency, make representations to the President and question decisions they consider unjust. Demands for a further presidential pardon should therefore be assessed with care and without assuming, in the absence of evidence, that the demand itself constitutes unlawful interference or establishes an improper motive.

Compassion or pursuit of partisan advantage

The Noble Eightfold Path nevertheless invites political leaders to examine the principles underlying their advocacy. Is the position grounded in compassion, fairness and the public interest? Is it consistent with principles applied in comparable cases? Does it acknowledge the interests of justice and the authority of the courts? Or might it be influenced by self-interest, political bias or the pursuit of partisan advantage?

Advocacy should inform rather than inflame

Right Speech is equally relevant. The medium, tone and methods of advocacy should be consistent with the Buddhist values being invoked: truthfulness, restraint, non-harm, compassion and respect for lawful institutions. Advocacy should inform rather than inflame, persuade rather than intimidate, and challenge decisions through responsible argument rather than personal vilification. These standards apply equally to political parties, religious authorities, public officials and citizens. They do not prohibit disagreement or compassionate appeals. They ask that the means adopted should be ethically consistent with the ends sought.

Constitutional responsibility

The demand for a second pardon also raises a question distinct from the ethical merits of political advocacy: what does the Constitution and the relevant judicial determination permit?

The Supreme Court’s decision invalidating the earlier pardon has made the constitutional context especially important. The UNP has stated that the ruling does not necessarily preclude a further pardon. That proposition must be considered in the light of the actual judgment and applicable constitutional requirements; it should not be accepted or rejected merely on the strength of a political statement. The distinction matters. A demand for clemency is not itself proof of illegality. Equally, compassion for an individual does not remove the need for a lawful and properly considered exercise of constitutional power. The legitimacy of any further decision depends on the governing law and the relevant facts, not simply on the strength of public pressure or the status of the person concerned.

World Buddhist Sangha Council’s 60th Anniversary

Here is an opportunity for wider Buddhist reflection, I thought. I noticed a news item about a preparatory meeting being held at the Presidential Secretariat on 26 October, chaired by senior representatives of the World Buddhist Sangha Council and the Secretary to the President, to review arrangements for its 60th anniversary celebrations and 11th General Conference, to be hosted in Sri-Lanka. The conference will take place from 28 November to 2 December 2026, commencing at the Nagananda International Institute for Buddhist Studies in Kelaniya, under the patronage of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake. Events are also planned for Anuradhapura and Kandy. More than 600 delegates are expected, including Buddhist monks from around the world, approximately 250 Sri Lankans living overseas and 250 Sri Lankan Buddhist monks.

A comparative discussion

Sri Lanka’s Buddhist institutions and political leaders could use the controversy about the robe, the demands for pardon, as an opportunity for broader reflection at this conference. If its program and arrangements permit, a comparative discussion could examine how different Buddhist traditions address allegations of misconduct, disciplinary inquiries, institutional independence and the relationship between monastic status and criminal accountability. Such a discussion should not seek to adjudicate an individual Sri Lankan case or impose a uniform disciplinary code on diverse traditions. Its purpose would be to exchange experience, identify sound practices and explore how the Sangha can preserve both its legitimate autonomy and the public trust on which its moral authority depends.

The test is consistency of principle

The Noble Eightfold Path does not provide a shortcut to resolving constitutional disputes, nor should Buddhist teaching be used selectively to legitimise a preferred political outcome. Its contribution is more fundamental: it asks individuals and institutions to examine their intentions, conduct and responsibilities with honesty. A monk’s robe should not confer immunity from accountability. Equally, a monk’s conviction should not justify hostility towards Buddhism or the Sangha as a whole. Political advocacy for clemency is legitimate within the democratic process, but its ethical quality depends on the principles and methods employed. Any Presidential decision must, in turn, satisfy the applicable constitutional requirements.

Ultimately, the question is not simply whether we support or oppose a particular pardon. It is whether we apply the same standards of compassion, fairness, accountability and lawful conduct when the individual concerned is someone we admire, someone we oppose, or someone whose cause offers political advantage. That is a test not only for the monk or the politician, but for all of us. It is also an opportunity to demonstrate that Buddhist ethical principles can inform public life without displacing the rule of law.

title: President pledges to crush narco ’shadow State’ and safeguard democracy and fundamental rights | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 7

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

Yes, we need an Act to prevent organised crime. The next question is whether the provisions in the Bill are too extensive or insufficient. We can discuss that. That is why we intend to inform the Supreme Court that we agree to three amendments. We have repeatedly indicated to the Supreme Court that we are prepared to amend these provisions. What we need is strong legislation to combat organised crime

Full text of speech delivered by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the religious summit held at Temple Trees on Thursday (5) to mark the first anniversary of the ‘Quit’ operation:

“Venerable members of the Maha Sangha and all other religious clergy have gathered here today with the aim of defeating a grave national menace. First of all, I wish to express our sincere gratitude to all of you for accepting our invitation and joining us on this occasion.

When I look at the thousands of members of the Maha Sangha and religious clergy gathered here, I am filled with the firm conviction that, however great the challenge before us may be, it can be overcome.

About a year ago, we launched a joint operation to defeat this menace. Drug seizures had been taking place all along, and various measures were being undertaken to overcome this threat. However, when we looked back at the statistics, what we saw was that drugs had continued to spread and increase. We therefore concluded that defeating this menace required a coordinated program. To that end, we appointed an operational committee representing all stakeholders.

We met several times during the year and took various decisions. Members of the Maha Sangha and religious clergy representing the National Council attended those meetings. Their support has consistently encouraged us. We can defeat this menace only through such a coordinated program.

Problem far deeper than appears

We made a promise to the people of this country that we would eradicate this menace from Sri Lanka entirely. We have gradually opened the doors to the extent of the destruction caused by it. The problem was far deeper than it appeared from the outside. We have therefore opened the doors of a cave filled with immense destruction. We know that there are people who have been unsettled by the opening of those doors. We now face two possible paths. One is to yield to those opposing this effort and abandon the journey. The other is to overcome whatever obstacles arise and bring to a successful conclusion the decision we have taken to defeat this menace. As a Government, we have chosen the second path. This menace must be defeated successfully.

This is the greatest menace afflicting our nation today. I know that different social groups have problems unique to them. However, irrespective of social divisions or cultural and linguistic differences, the national menace confronting all of us is the drug menace. We must save our nation from this scourge. We must therefore continue on this path.

A large quantity of drugs was seized during operations last year. The total quantity of drugs seized by us during this year amounts to 438,330 kilograms.

In 2022, only one person under the age of 18 was arrested in connection with the drug known as ‘Ice’. By 2025, however, we had arrested 1,874. We have also arrested 11,737 young people over the age of 21. Among this group, 10,889 were between 18 and 21 years of age. There were also 1,068 children aged between 14 and 18, and 13 children aged between five and 14. This means that even very young children have fallen victim to this menace. More than 200 girls have also been arrested.

This menace is destroying our entire younger generation and our future. Those of us who love and care about our country and nation, and who have hopes for the future of our young people, cannot remain silent in the face of this. We have one task before us: to defeat it.

All these figures demonstrate the scale of this menace. In addition, during this year we have seized 15,282 kg, of narcotic drugs. This includes 6,528 kg, of ‘Ice’ and 4,000 kg, of heroin. This morning, too, 150 kg of heroin and ‘Ice’ were seized. We have also seized 2,598 kg of other drugs, 1,841 kg of hashish, 314 kg of cocaine, and nearly 4.5 million drug tablets and capsules.

The total value of the drugs we have seized is Rs. 218 billion. When cannabis is included, the value rises to Rs. 224 billion. This is the drug market for a single year. When we also take into account the quantities that have not been seized, the enormous scale of the destruction becomes clear.

Shadow State emerges

A powerful network has been built around this drug trade, which is worth around Rs. 220 billion. We cannot rid our country of drugs without dismantling this network. The enormous wealth generated by this trade has enabled drug traffickers to buy off public officials, some officers of the Customs Department, officials of the Department of Motor Traffic, immigration officers, certain police officers, as well as businesspeople and even politicians. In the past, leading drug traffickers were able to secure positions as chairpersons and members of local authorities. They began building political movements with the enormous wealth they had accumulated through the drug trade.

Today, this menace is engulfing the entire society. There is no longer any institution that remains untouched. It is spreading into religious institutions that are revered and respected. For more than 2,000 years, the Maha Sangha and the Sangha community have travelled from village to village, often wearing out their feet, to help build our society. This menace has reached them, to varying degrees, as well. It has also spread to other religious institutions. The Police, the three armed forces and State institutions have all been affected.

In place of the State machinery that is visible to us, a ‘shadow State’ operating from within has emerged. If this continues to grow, all the mechanisms that uphold a respected society, sustain public hope and bring order to society will become ineffective. The enormous illicit wealth they accumulate gives them the ability to take control of all these institutions. I say once again that we have two paths before us.

They can remain within their shadow State, while we continue carrying out the work entrusted to us within the State. That is how many people have conducted themselves. However, as a Government, we have taken a decision: we will defeat this shadow State and dismantle it. Our children cannot have a secure future unless we dismantle the shadow State linked to drugs. How much hope do parents place in raising their children? Parents spend most of their lives on their children – to give them a good life, a good future and a safe society. How hard they work. I do not think there is a mother or father anywhere in the world who works harder for their children.

Dismantling criminal machinery

In a country where parents work so hard to secure a good future for their children, they are now confronted with a question before their very eyes: do those children actually have a secure future? I know that a large number of parents feel helpless in the face of this menace. It is spreading throughout society like a giant monster. The drug network associated with it and the criminal machinery connected to that network must be dismantled. Under the ‘Ratama Ekata’ (A Nation United) program, we drew up plans to dismantle this criminal State. As a result, we have been able to arrest organised criminals linked to the drug network within Sri Lanka and bring back those who had fled the country.

This year, we arrested individuals known by various aliases who had terrorised towns and villages. We brought 67 people who were overseas back to Sri Lanka. Going forward, wherever in the world they may be hiding, if they are involved in organised crime connected to the drug trade in our country, we say to them: ‘You are not safe, wherever you may be.’ We have also issued Red Notices for 112 people and frozen assets worth 4,500 million.

We have frozen assets worth 4,500 million that were acquired through drug trafficking. During this year, 97 T-56 automatic firearms have been seized. That is a quantity that may even exceed what some police stations have available. Some of these firearms have come out of our armed forces; this has been revealed through audit reports. On certain occasions, we received reports that a police officer had sold a firearm and fled. Firearms had found their way out. We have seized 143 pistols, 47 AK-47 rifles and 105 revolvers. These are the quantities of firearms held by the criminal State. We believe there are more.

When such a quantity of firearms is in the hands of criminals, is our society safe? Are our children safe? Our children are not safe in this society. So many firearms are moving around freely, and more must be seized. We have drawn up plans to address this. That is why we are conducting a major operation to suppress this drug network.

In particular, the Inspector-General of Police and the Police Department, together with the Commander of the Navy, the Commander of the Air Force, the Commander of the Army and the wider military apparatus, are making a tremendous effort in this operation, in these arrests and in defeating this menace.”

These institutions are engaged in a major operation to save the State and protect our children. Yet, instead of recognising these operations, if an officer makes some mistake, it becomes a newspaper headline and the main item on a television channel’s news program.

Who has made the effort to seize drugs worth nearly Rs. 220 billion and to confiscate such large quantities of firearms? It is the Police and the three armed forces. Our Government will therefore give due recognition to the work they have done in this operation. We have also taken steps to provide bonuses and incentives to many officers who took part in operations in the recent past, and we will consider further measures in this regard.

The support of the police and the three armed forces is essential for these operations. However, arrests alone are not enough; we also need a rehabilitation program. We have newly established rehabilitation centres in areas such as Batticaloa, Akuressa, Nittambuwa and Kandy. We have also improved existing rehabilitation centres in areas such as Kandakadu, Senapura and Vavuniya. In addition, our plans are not limited to rehabilitation centres funded entirely by the State. Temples, religious clergy and civil society organisations also operate a number of rehabilitation centres. We are ready to provide the fullest possible Government support to those centres. We are prepared to work with them and provide the assistance they need.

In addition, with the involvement of our Department of Health and a large number of relevant institutions, 259,000 community awareness programs on prevention have been organised across the country. We have conducted a large number of such programs to educate the public and children.

Strengthening laws

We must suppress this menace within the framework of the law. We have absolutely no intention of stepping outside the legal framework in the process of defeating it. We have laws in place, and we operate under those laws. If the law is inadequate, we will make new laws. There was a major issue concerning the destruction of seized drugs. There was widespread public suspicion: large quantities of drugs were being shown as seized, but were these drugs subsequently finding their way back on to the market?

Under the legal framework that existed, we had no authority to destroy seized items until a case filed in court had concluded and the court had issued an order to destroy the items concerned. We have, however, enacted the legislation required to enable their destruction.

Next, there was no law to confiscate wealth and assets acquired through drugs – in other words, proceeds and assets acquired unlawfully. Therefore, in 2025, we passed the law on the confiscation of unlawfully acquired assets. It is under this confiscation law that assets worth Rs. 4.5 billion have now been confiscated from criminals. Had that law not existed, we would have had no opportunity to seize those assets.

Another matter now under discussion is the Organised Crime Bill. At present, we enforce the law against organised criminals under the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). That is the reality. When an organised criminal attempts to escape from custody, we have sought to bring the attempted escape under the law through the Prevention of Terrorism Act. But what is the act in question? It is an organised criminal attempting to escape from custody. Under the law currently in force, investigations had to be conducted and charges brought under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. As there was no other option, we attempted to file cases under the PTA.

We intend to substantially weaken the PTA – the Prevention of Terrorism Act. This is because we do not currently face terrorist activity on a day-to-day basis. We will make it a much weaker Act. There is a discussion on this, and we are talking about it. However, we need strong legislation to prevent organised crime. This is the law required in this era to free the nation from this menace.

The law is constantly evolving. New laws are enacted in response to new challenges. There was a time when there were no environmental laws. However, when the environment began to suffer serious damage, laws were enacted to protect it. There was a time when there were no money-laundering laws. But when the accumulation of illicit wealth became a major threat, the Money Laundering Act was introduced. There was a time when rulers did not destroy public property. But when rulers began destroying public property, legislation was introduced to protect it. Organised crime has now grown. Therefore, an Act to prevent organised crime is necessary in this era.

The law is not eternal. A law enacted today will not remain in force for all time. New challenges emerge in society. When new challenges arise, strong laws are needed to address them.

At the very beginning of this program, a year ago, we said that if the laws available to punish these individuals were inadequate, we would introduce new laws. That is what a Government is for. Citizens cannot make these laws. An ordinary person cannot make them, nor can a Grama Niladhari officer. If such a law is to be enacted, the authority lies with Parliament and nowhere else. Parliament has the power to legislate.

Protecting democracy and fundamental rights

Today, we need strong legislation to prevent organised crime. We have now presented the Bill to Parliament. There are two groups opposing this legislation. One is quite clear: those who receive privileges and protection from organised criminals. We do not take that group into consideration. But there is another group – those who speak about democracy and the fundamental rights of the people of our country. We are ready to discuss the matter with that group.

Our intention is in no way to suppress the people or deprive them of their rights. We need legislation to combat organised crime, and we are prepared to enact it. The Bill is currently before the Supreme Court and is under consideration. Those who have challenged the Bill before the Court have, at this stage, raised three main issues.

One concerns the period of detention. Under this Bill, the detention period is 72 hours. It has been proposed that this is too long. There is a discussion on this before our Supreme Court. We are prepared to amend it and reduce the period from 72 hours to 48 hours. We are ready to listen. There is another matter under discussion concerning internationally recognised organised gangs identified by tattoos. There is an international trend towards identifying such gangs. If our country does not have a law to address this, and if we do not need such a provision at present, we are prepared to remove it.

There is another provision stating that offences committed under the Excise Ordinance can also be dealt with under the Organised Crime Act. We will remove that provision too, making it clear that offences under the Excise Ordinance will not be dealt with under the Organised Crime Act. There is no problem with that. These are the three main issues in the Bill currently being discussed before the Supreme Court. If there are any others, we are ready to consider them.

What these laws could mean when we are no longer in power?

This is in no way about obtaining undue powers for me, the Government, the police or our departments. Why do we need these powers? No one holds power forever. Whenever we exercise power, we must do so with the mindset that we should be ready to relinquish it. When we exercise power, we must always consider the laws we enact by asking ourselves: what would these laws mean when we are no longer in power? We are not acting with the intention of retaining power for the long term or with the mindset that we will never give it up. 

We act knowing that the people have entrusted power to us, and that they can take it back at any time – they can do so through an election. We know that. Therefore, in exercising power, we have no agenda involving me, my children or my relatives.

There is no such agenda. That is why we are prepared to amend the law. But the first question we must settle through discussion is this: do we need an Organised Crime Act or not? Do we need an Act to prevent organised crime? I believe that everyone, except those who receive protection or privileges from organised criminals, would answer ‘yes’. Yes, we need an Act to prevent organised crime. The next question is whether the provisions in the Bill are too extensive or insufficient. We can discuss that. That is why we intend to inform the Supreme Court that we agree to three amendments. We have repeatedly indicated to the Supreme Court that we are prepared to amend these provisions. What we need is strong legislation to combat organised crime. 

However, the law alone is not enough. Ultimately, once an organised criminal or drug trafficker is arrested, that person must be brought before the law and punished. As a Government, we do not follow a policy of imposing punishment outside the law. That has happened in the past. We will under no circumstances punish anyone outside the law. A law is required, and the case must be heard and punishment imposed in accordance with that law.

However, trials take too long. That cannot continue. Those institutions must therefore be strengthened. The institutions conducting investigations must be strengthened; the Attorney General’s Department, which files cases, must be strengthened; the Government Analyst’s Department, which provides the scientific evidence required for those cases, must be strengthened; and the judicial sector, which ultimately hears those cases, must also be strengthened. We are intervening in all these areas. 

We have made plans to improve investigative institutions and the police, and to provide them with specialised training. Investigations must be conducted, and cases must be filed on the basis of those investigations. For that, the Attorney General’s Department must be strengthened. In particular, we need Government Analyst’s reports. Our Government Analyst is here, and we need those reports. We had a backlog of 36,000 reports.

Normally, only around 3,000 reports were completed a month. We deployed additional staff and provided new allowances. Our Navy also assisted with some infrastructure requirements. What did we do by providing assistance with infrastructure?

We only need engineers, designers, workers and raw materials to demolish a building and construct a new one. That is a task for a small team. A team can also build a large reservoir. But defeating this menace requires the support of the people. You know your child well: you can recognise whether your child has fallen victim to this, whether your spouse is becoming involved, whether changes in behaviour are emerging, whether your child is becoming a member of the underworld, or whether your child is becoming involved in this menace. Before a police officer makes an arrest, parents know whether their child is a drug user or a drug trafficker. Do they not? Because of the relationship between parents and children, it is very difficult for this to happen without parents knowing. Parents therefore have a major role to play in confronting this menace. In particular, through the Ministry of Education, we are developing a program not for children, but for parents.

We must explain to parents what happens when their children’s futures are destroyed. What happens when someone becomes addicted to drugs? The mind becomes confused, the body becomes emaciated, self-respect is lost, personality breaks down, the person is marginalised by society and, ultimately, the death penalty may be imposed under the law. If we strengthen this law, the ultimate penalty will be death – that is what the law provides. Parents who love their children must understand this: a child may initially become attracted to drugs, but what is the eventual outcome? The death penalty under the law. 

Parents therefore have a responsibility to prevent their beloved children from falling victim to this menace. I know that when a family faces such a tragedy, mothers and fathers rush to tell the Venerable Thero: ‘Our Venerable Thero, we never imagined that my younger son or my elder son would end up like this.’ They say, ‘We never thought this would happen to my husband.’ Otherwise, they go to their church, their priest or their Kurukkal. We know that, at the outset, parents do not come directly to the police.

Mothers and fathers are more open with religious leaders or with doctors. They do speak to doctors to some extent. However, they are more likely to open up to our Buddhist monks and other religious clergy. Therefore, the first to hear about and witness the distressing consequences of this menace in a village are often the monks and religious clergy of that village.

Role of religion

I therefore believe that, in defeating a menace of this nature, while the police, the armed forces and the State machinery constitute the formal institutional response we have chosen as a society, the responsibility for providing wider social and ideological guidance beyond the formal system rests, in my view, with our Venerable monks.

How many people do you meet in a day, a month or a year? How many sermons do you deliver? How many times do you advise children and parents? How often do you listen to their grief and suffering? I believe this is where our first line of defence lies. Our Venerable monks, together with the other religious clergy, are the principal force in providing the social leadership needed to defeat this menace.

Many people have gathered here today. I believe this is one of the largest gatherings of Buddhist monks in one place in Sri Lanka in recent times. A large number of our Maulavis are also attending. Our priests and Kurukkals have come here from Jaffna. Some of the Kurukkals who left Jaffna yesterday have arrived here today. What does that demonstrate? It shows us your commitment. But what is needed now? I repeat: if the State alone could do this, we would not be holding a conference of this nature. We would simply summon State officials and speak to them. 

The State cannot do this alone. Everyone’s contribution and organised involvement are necessary. We will give this priority: we will enact the necessary laws, strengthen institutions, ensure that courts are equipped to hear cases, make the police and armed forces effective, and establish our rehabilitation authority and institutions. That is the Government’s responsibility. However, the greatest role in defeating this menace belongs to the general public.

I also believe that our Venerable monks have a major role to play in this regard. I therefore ask you to become active participants in this effort. I know that we have held discussions from time to time with the Anunayake Theros of the Asgiriya and Malwathu Chapters, the Registrar of the Amarapura Maha Nikaya and the Anunayake Thero of the Ramanna Maha Nikaya. During the past year, we have met on seven occasions, with each discussion lasting two and a half to three hours, to consider how to defeat this menace. Our Kurukkals, Maulavis and other religious clergy have participated in large numbers and have consistently put forward proposals with great enthusiasm to overcome it. We must now turn this into a major national movement. What do we need today? Let us set aside those political divisions.

Let us set aside all our other divisions as well. Above those divisions, we must recognise only two sides: those who support the drugs trade, armed criminal gangs and the criminal State built around them, and those who oppose them. That is all. There should be no other division in the country today.

Today, this monster called drugs has spread throughout the country, leaving no place untouched. This menace has grown over several decades because it was supported, ignored or simply allowed to continue. We are now tasked with defeating a menace that has already grown to enormous proportions. We know what needs to be done to address it, but this is no longer at the beginning. It has now become a massive national crisis. This is not something that can be brought to an end in a year or two. However, if we continue this effort without giving up for several years, we can free our nation from this menace. We can create a secure future for our younger generation and a safe society, free from conflict. We can build a country in which our children can live with pride. I believe that our Venerable monks have a great responsibility in this endeavour. I invite and appeal to you to become partners and active participants in this effort.”

title: Taxation, fairness and the public purse | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 7 November 2026 00:00
-     - 10

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The true measure of a successful fiscal policy is not how much money a Government manages to collect or borrow, but how effectively it converts public resources into national prosperity, economic opportunity and social well-being

Taxation is an instrument of governance, not an entitlement to extract

Among the many  expectations placed on a national Budget, taxation policy occupies a particularly important position. This consideration assumes even greater significance in a country where the prevailing tax rates are already relatively  high, placing a considerable burden on individuals, households and business alike.

The legitimacy of taxation rests not merely on the authority of a Government to impose taxes, but on the reasoning, fairness and public purpose behind such decisions.

Governments require revenue to maintain public services, protect citizens, develop infrastructure and fulfil their responsibilities. No responsible society can dispute that necessity. However, the more important question is whether the methods adopted to raise revenue are economically sensible, socially equitable and consistent with the long-term interests of the nation.

This is a question that deserves particular attention in modern economies, where governments increasingly rely on taxation, borrowing and elaborate Budgetary projections to finance their commitments.

The wisdom of ancient statecraft

It is interesting to revisit the principles advocated by Kautilya, also known as Chanakya, the celebrated Indian strategist and author of the Arthashastra.

Kautilya recognised the importance of a strong treasury as an essential foundation of state power. Yet his approach to revenue collection was not simply one of maximising the State’s income.

He emphasised that taxation should be administered with prudence and should not undermine the productive capacity of the people. His analogy of collecting the fruits of a garden when they ripen, rather than taking them prematurely, illustrates a principle of enduring economic relevance. The more common version is comparing it to a bee gathering honey from a flower without molesting it.

The underlying message is particularly important: a ruler must not weaken the very economic foundation from which public revenue is generated.

The same principle can be applied to modern taxation. Excessive or poorly designed taxation can discourage investment, reduce consumption, weaken enterprise, drive economic activity into informality and ultimately erode the very tax base that the Government seeks to expand.

A Government must therefore understand the difference between collecting more revenue and creating greater national wealth.

Fairness must be the foundation

Taxation should be guided by the ability-to-pay principle, economic capacity and the equitable distribution of the national burden.

Those with greater financial capacity may reasonably be expected to contribute more. However, fairness cannot be measured simply by the nominal tax rate imposed on different categories of taxpayers.

The combined impact of direct taxes, indirect taxes, levies and other charges must also be considered.

A salaried employee paying income tax, a small entrepreneur struggling with operating costs, and a low-income household paying consumption taxes experience the tax system in very different ways.

Indirect taxation can be particularly burdensome on ordinary households because a greater proportion of their limited income is spent on essential goods and services.

It is therefore insufficient to claim that a tax system is equitable merely because it applies the same rate to everyone within a particular category.

The real test is whether the overall burden is reasonable, proportionate and sensitive to the economic circumstances of those who bear it.

The modern Budget: Estimates, assumptions and realities

The preparation of a national Budget is an exercise in economic planning and financial discipline. It should be based on realistic revenue estimates, clearly identified expenditure requirements, credible economic projections and an honest assessment of the country’s capacity to finance its commitments.

Yet modern Budget-making can sometimes become excessively dependent on projections and assumptions.

Expected increases in revenue, anticipated improvements in economic activity, projected investment inflows and estimated savings are often incorporated into financial plans before their actual realisation.

There is nothing inherently wrong with forecasting. Every Budget must look ahead. The danger arises when optimistic assumptions are treated as dependable financial resources and expenditure commitments are built around them.

A Budget should distinguish clearly between revenue already secured, revenue reasonably expected and revenue that remains conditional upon future economic developments.

Where the assumptions fail to materialise, the consequences cannot simply be transferred to the public through additional taxation or indiscriminate borrowing.

Borrowing is not revenue

One of the most important distinctions in responsible public finance is the difference between revenue and borrowed money.

Tax revenue represents a contribution collected by the State under law. Borrowing, on the other hand, creates an obligation that must ultimately be serviced and repaid, or refinanced at a future cost.

Borrowing is not necessarily undesirable. Governments may legitimately borrow to finance economically productive infrastructure, investments that generate future returns, or extraordinary circumstances requiring temporary financial support.

However, borrowing to sustain recurring expenditure, meet unrealistic Budgetary commitments or compensate indefinitely for deficiencies in revenue generation is a fundamentally different proposition.

The danger is that governments may create the appearance of financial capacity by continuously adding liabilities to the public purse.

There is no unlimited reservoir of borrowing. Every additional liability carries interest costs, repayment obligations, exchange-rate exposure where foreign currency is involved, and a corresponding reduction in the fiscal room available to future governments.

A Budget cannot be considered balanced in any meaningful economic sense merely because a financing gap has been filled through additional borrowing.

The danger of hypothetical balancing

A particularly important issue is the manner in which governments reconcile their expenditure commitments with anticipated revenue and borrowing requirements.

If projected revenue is uncertain, expenditure estimates are insufficiently disciplined and the resulting deficit is covered through borrowing, the apparent financial equilibrium may be more a product of accounting assumptions than genuine economic strength.

The question is not simply whether the Treasury can raise the required funds today. It is whether the economy can sustain the resulting obligations tomorrow.

Responsible Budget-making must therefore incorporate alternative scenarios, sensitivity analysis, debt-servicing capacity and an assessment of the risks associated with revenue shortfalls.

The International Monetary Fund’s principles of fiscal transparency similarly emphasise realistic Budgets, medium-term fiscal frameworks and disclosure of fiscal risks.

Sri Lanka’s particular responsibility

Sri Lanka’s recent economic experience makes these principles especially relevant.

The country has undergone a severe economic and debt crisis, followed by difficult fiscal adjustments, revenue-enhancement measures and debt restructuring.

The Public Financial Management Act, No. 44 of 2024, and the Public Debt Management Act, No. 33 of 2024, establish important institutional and legal frameworks for fiscal accountability and debt management. The Economic Transformation Act, No. 45 of 2024, also provides statutory fiscal objectives.

These measures recognise that public finance cannot be managed indefinitely through discretionary decisions and short-term Budgetary expedients.

Nevertheless, legislation and numerical targets alone cannot guarantee responsible financial management. Their effectiveness ultimately depends on the quality of the assumptions, the discipline exercised in implementing them, transparency in reporting and the willingness to correct policies when circumstances change.

Sri Lanka must also recognise that fiscal consolidation cannot be viewed exclusively through the revenue collected by the Treasury. The ability of households to sustain consumption, businesses to invest, industries to expand and exporters to compete is equally important.

An economy cannot tax its way into prosperity if the productive capacity required to generate future income and employment is weakened in the process.

The responsibility of Government

The responsibility of a Government is not simply to balance the figures presented in an annual Budget. It is to protect and expand the nation’s economic capacity while ensuring that the burden of financing the State is distributed fairly.

Every major tax measure should therefore be examined against several fundamental questions:

These are not unreasonable demands from taxpayers. They are essential requirements of an accountable Government.

Conclusion: Protecting the roots of national prosperity

The wisdom of ancient statecraft and the principles of modern public finance converge on one fundamental truth: the strength of a State ultimately depends on the strength of its people and the productive economy that sustains them.

Taxation must not destroy the capacity to create wealth. Borrowing must not become a permanent substitute for financial discipline. Budgets must not be built on hypothetical expectations while actual obligations are passed on to future generations.

A Government should collect what is reasonably necessary, spend what it can responsibly afford, borrow for defensible purposes and account openly for every major financial decision.

The true measure of a successful fiscal policy is not how much money a Government manages to collect or borrow, but how effectively it converts public resources into national prosperity, economic opportunity and social well-being.

title: Adhil, Wihanga propel Asoka College to maiden All-Island rugby title | Daily FT
summary:

-     - 1

The victorious Asoka College Under-14 rugby team with school Principal Buddika Attanayake, Vice Principal, coaching staff and school rugby officials

Player of the Tournament Asoka College’s Adhil Naushad who scored eight tries

Asoka College, Colombo, scripted a golden chapter in their rugby history, by clinching the All-Island Under-14 Premier Rugby Sevens Championship 2026 with a thrilling 28-21 victory over Dudley Senanayake MV in a fiercely contested Cup final played at Hettipola Public grounds, Kurunegala.

Organised by the Sri Lanka Schools Rugby Football Association (SLSRFA), the tournament featured 32 schools, with the young Asokians producing an unbeaten campaign to secure their first-ever All-Island rugby title, a landmark achievement coming a decade after the school finished runners-up in the Under-14 Milo Cup 10-a-side competition.

The final was a pulsating encounter, with both sides displaying attacking flair, determined defence and exceptional schoolboy rugby. However, Asoka’s clinical finish and teamwork ultimately proved decisive.

The defining passage of play came through a brilliantly executed pass involving scrum-half Sasath Sandiv and prop Thehas Bandara, with fly-half Adhil Naushad putting the finishing touches to the decisive try.

Captain Wihanga Pansilu Ashinsa also produced a moment of individual brilliance, powering through two defenders to cross the white line. Naushad was undoubtedly Asoka’s attacking spearhead, running in eight tries throughout the tournament. Skipper Pansilu was equally influential with six tries, while Bandara added two and Aathik Naushad contributed another. Sanuth Dasanayake also crossed the try line and provided valuable conversions.

Scrum-half Sandiv was outstanding, combining intelligent distribution with several crucial, try-saving tackles. His quick service repeatedly created scoring opportunities for Naushad and the outside backs.

Winger Sanuj Nethuka and replacement scrum-half Maheesha Sadev made valuable contributions whenever called upon, demonstrating the squad’s impressive depth. Emerging players Resath Silva, Shabir Ahamed and Saven Themika also showed considerable promise after graduating from Under-12 rugby.

The Asokians opened their campaign by overwhelming Panadura Royal College 35-0 before defeating Rangiri Dambulla Vidyalaya 35-7. Following a walkover against Eheliyagoda Central College, they swept aside tournament favourites S. Thomas’ Preparatory School, Kollupitiya 28-7.

A commanding 42-12 quarter-final victory over Athugalpura Kumara Vidyalaya paved the way for their memorable Cup final triumph.

Asoka College Principal Buddika Attanayake hailed the achievement as a defining moment for the school’s sporting ambitions.

“This historic victory reflects the determination of our young players and the collective commitment of our coaches, teachers and parents. Winning our first All-Island rugby title is an immense source of pride and an inspiration for future generations of Asokians,” he said.

Coach Suranga Arunashantha, a former Air Force rugby player and national-level referee with development squad experience in 2000–01, credited the team’s discipline and collective spirit to the win.

“These boys played with tremendous courage and belief. Adhil’s finishing and Wihanga’s leadership were outstanding, but our real strength was teamwork, particularly Sasath’s intelligent distribution and committed defence. Completing the tournament unbeaten makes this achievement truly special,” he said.

The starting seven comprised Wihanga Pansilu Ashinsa, Thehas Bandara, Isuka Siriwardana, Sasath Sandiv, Adhil Naushad, Sanuth Nethmira and Chenuk Sandil.

Asoka’s achievement was supported by Masters-in-Charge Nuwan Abeysinghe and Mrs. Hasitha Premaratne, Vice Principal Chamara Adipaththu, Prefect of Games Sagarika Kulatunga and Principal Attanayake, alongside the unwavering dedication of parents.

Dudley Senanayake MV finished Cup runners-up, while S. Thomas’ Preparatory School claimed the Shield and Nalanda College, Colombo, secured the Bowl.

ISLAMABAD: Off-spinner Keshara Nuwantha impressed with both bat and ball to give Sri Lanka a morale-boosting 142-run win against PCB Patron’s XI in their only 3-day warm-up match concluded at the Islamabad Club Cricket Oval here yesterday.

Nuwantha first contributed a valuable 30 runs batting at number 8 to help Sri Lanka extend their overall lead to 253. Then came back with the ball to capture four wickets. The chase collapsed rapidly under a clinical performance from the young Sri Lankan bowling attack.

The Patrons XI were dismantled for just 111 runs as Nuwantha led the destruction with outstanding figures of 4/26 in 7 overs. He was brilliantly supported by Eshan Malinga, who tore through the remaining line-up with a blistering spell of 3 wickets for just 6 runs in 3.1 overs. Dilshan Madushanka wrapped up the performance by claiming 1/15 to seal the victory for Sri Lanka giving them a strong confidence booster ahead of the upcoming 2-Test series against Pakistan starting at Rawalpindi on 9 November.

Sri Lanka resumed the final day on 121-6 and added 60 runs to their total before being bowled out for 181, setting the home side a target of 254 runs. Milan Rathnayaka carried his overnight total of 27 to 40 of 77 balls (5 fours) and Nuwantha contributed 30.
